title: “Astonishing” Find: Fossilized Dinosaur Blood in a 115-Million-Year-Old Specimen - Nautilus
gist: Paywall-truncated report on a PNAS study that identified fossilized, cell-sized blood structures in the leg bone of a 115-million-year-old juvenile theropod, Aratasaurus museunacionali, from a Brazilian mine. This is presented as a step forward for molecular paleontology.

insights.claim: A team of paleontologists and geochemists reported in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences that they found fossilized blood cells in a 115-million-year-old dinosaur specimen.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
entities: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
insights.so_what: Preserved soft tissue in deep time is now verifiable, which widens what molecular paleontology can study.

insights.claim: The blood cells came from the hind leg bone of a juvenile Cretaceous-era theropod, Aratasaurus museunacionali, which was excavated from a Brazilian mine in 2008.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Specimens dug up years ago can yield new discoveries when reexamined with better tools.

insights.claim: Researchers cut thin slices of the fossilized bone, treated them chemically and inspected them under an electron microscope. They found round blobs roughly the size of cells, confined to vascular channels that once held blood vessels.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Shows how imaging and geochemistry methods are improving in paleontology.
insights.quote: The blobs were localized to vascular channels that would have carried blood vessels when the dinosaur was alive.

insights.claim: Molecular paleontology is steadily improving its ability to recover biological traces from deep-time fossils.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Watch for more soft-tissue and biomolecule finds as the techniques mature.
